Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Ellis: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick check, can you all hear me ok?
[00:03] Eva Chen: yeah hearing you, thanks.
[00:06] Markus Vogel: good.
[00:10] Jordan: cool. objective for today is a short Optimize walkthrough — specifically batching and the prefix / K V cache recommendations tied back to a cost model. we'll try not to get too deep into model selection unless you want.
[00:21] Sara N'dour: that's perfect. our main ask is: can we get to predictable p95 under 300ms without blowing the budget, and also retain privacy controls.
[00:30] Samir Rao: great. quick qual: what's your current qps and typical seq length distribution?
[00:35] Eva: right now peak is about 450 qps, average session has a prompt of 80 tokens then a 40-token followup, so think typical turn is ~120 tokens but with a long tail to 600 on help sessions.
[00:48] Markus: infra is currently EKS on CloudX, Redis for sessions, we do not want to put customer data in third-party unless encrypted; we have a KMS in CloudX and use SAML SSO.
[00:58] Jordan: ok noted. so two immediate levers: batching / concurrency and prefix/KV cache. in Redwood Optimize we usually map expected qps + seq distribution to an economic model — that trades off with latency SLOs.
[01:12] Samir: to set expectations: continuous batching is great for throughput but can increase tail latencies if not tuned; session affinity and small-batch fast-paths help. we also have dynamic batch sizing in the runtime.
[01:26] Eva: can you run through a concrete example — like we have 450 peak qps and those lengths, what would you recommend for batch size and cache hit rates?
[01:34] Jordan: sure. i'll share a simplified cost sim. imagine without prefix caching you get no KV hits, so per-token cost is higher and p95 spikes. with a 20% KV hit rate on the first 128 tokens you can drop per-request token compute by roughly 12-18% depending on model.
[01:47] Markus: sorry can i interrupt — when you say K V hits, is that the prefix cache for session history or you mean the KV from a reranker?
[01:54] Samir: good call — in our terminology prefix/KV cache is the key-value activation cache that stores past attention contexts (the 'prefix') so subsequent tokens can reuse KV state. it's not Redis session data. sometimes transcription or doc notes call it 'kay-vee cache' — same thing.
[02:08] Eva: ok got it.
[02:12] Jordan: right. recommendation one: set a short TTL for prefix cache entries for conversational flows — 5 to 15 minutes depending on session churn — longer for persistent sessions like docs. that increases hit rate on short-return followups but avoids unbounded memory.
[02:28] Eva: how does TTL interact with cold-start for a user returning after 30 minutes?
[02:32] Samir: if TTL expired, we fall back to full context regen. Optimize has a prefetch suggestion: if we detect high probability of return within 1-5 minutes (based on signals), we can pre-warm the KV cache during quiet periods. it's a low-cost prefetch because it's only prefix encoding.
[02:46] Markus: what's the cost of prefetching at scale? we are sensitive to extra compute.
[02:51] Jordan: good question. in the cost model we amortize prefetch cost by expected hit probability. if prefetch increases hit rate by 15% and costs 3% extra compute, net wins. we'll share a workbook that calculates this.
[03:05] Sara: curious about batching — you mentioned dynamic batch sizing, is there an option to prioritize latency over throughput for certain routes? we have a high-value route for payment verifications where p95 must be low.
[03:16] Samir: yes, route-level policies in Redwood Console. you can pin critical routes to a lower-batch, lower-latency policy (prefer single-request fast-path), and let other routes use larger batch sizes. also can set fallback to a faster, smaller model if the big model is saturated.
[03:32] Eva: any sample numbers you can share now? like p50/p95 at 450 qps with default policies vs with pv caching?
[03:38] Jordan: high level: default no-cache at 450 qps on our hosted endpoints for a medium LLM we typically see p50 ~60-90ms and p95 in the 220-320ms range depending on batching. with a 25% KV hit and moderate batching we can often nudge p95 under 200ms while lowering compute cost ~10-15%. caveat: depends on seq length tail.
[03:59] Markus: you said hosted endpoints — we might prefer dedicated or private for compliance later. does the Optimize model change?
[04:06] Samir: the optimizations are identical: runtime supports the same continuous batching and KV cache semantics across hosted, dedicated, and private. the difference is capacity and network layer; private deployments can reduce network latency and give you KMS in your VPC.
[04:20] Eva: what's required for private — is it an on-prem install or a VPC-managed control plane?
[04:25] Jordan: both options. Private can be VPC-hosted control plane with customer-managed worker nodes, or fully on-prem package. both integrate with SAML, KMS/HSM. we'll include the architecture doc in the security pack.
[04:36] Sara: security — SOC2 and audit logs are musts. do you surface per-request audit logs?
[04:41] Samir: yes, Console has token-level tracing and retention options; audit logs can be exported to your SIEM. we support customer-managed KMS so payloads can be encrypted at rest. note: audit logs themselves may include metadata; we can redact or route them to private sinks.
[04:58] Jordan: back to cost: one of the unique things in Optimize is the integrated cost simulation. you feed in your traffic profile, we model batching, prefetch, TTL, and show estimated vCPU/GPU-hours and token compute. it's not perfect but gives directional guidance.
[05:12] Eva: do you support mixed-precision quantization recommendations? we are considering 4-bit quant for cheaper inference.
[05:18] Samir: yes we can recommend quant profiles per-model per-workload. caveat: 4-bit often gives good cost savings but you need to check quality regressions; our Optimize console can run small evals on your prompt sets.
[05:31] Markus: can you show the console quickly?
[05:33] Jordan: sure, switching screenshare...
[05:35] [screen share noise - brief silence]
[05:37] Jordan: ok visible? this is the Optimize sandbox. here's the traffic profile input — we've preloaded a sample similar to your numbers. you can see expected qps, seq-length histogram, session reentry probabilities.
[05:50] Jordan: first chart is the baseline cost without KV cache. second chart toggles prefix caching at various TTLs. notice how the model cost line drops as hit rate increases.
[06:02] Eva: that hover tooltip shows p95 — what's the assumed batch window?
[06:06] Samir: default batch window is 40ms but can be tuned. smaller windows reduce batching but lower latency; bigger windows increase throughput efficiency. in the sim we sweep windows from 20ms to 80ms.
[06:18] Markus: the sim also lists burst autoscale costs? our traffic spikes 2x during sales events.
[06:24] Jordan: yep, we model burst capacity and dedicated pools. you can specify reserved throughput and expected burst pattern; the cost sim outputs both steady-state and peak costs. for your 2x spikes, we typically recommend a modest reserved commit plus burst autoscale.
[06:37] Eva: about warmup strategies — you mentioned prefetch earlier. is it better to prefetch prefixes for likely-returning sessions or to maintain longer TTLs?
[06:45] Samir: tradeoff: longer TTLs increase memory and may hold stale KV. prefetching is targeted and cheaper if we have a good return probability signal. we often combine both: short TTL (e.g., 10m) + targeted prefetch when predicted return prob > 40% within next 2 minutes.
[07:01] Sara: interesting. how do you get return probability? is that built-in or needs customer signal?
[07:06] Jordan: can be both. Console supports simple heuristics (e.g., user idle < 2m and recent interaction pattern) and you can provide a custom signal via an API call to Redwood Optimize to indicate likely-return.
[07:18] Eva: can we control route-level cache policies via API? we have complex routing rules.
[07:22] Samir: yes. Console exposes route configs and you can set cache TTL, allowlist/denylist, prefetch policies per route via API or via the UI. good for sensitive routes where you want no caching.
[07:35] Markus: what about multi-region routing — our users are global. will KV cache hits be regional?
[07:40] Jordan: yes KV cache is region-scoped; we recommend routing requests for a given user to the same region (session affinity) to maximize hits. the smart routing layer can enforce session affinity for small latency cost.
[07:52] Eva: if we do session affinity, what's failover behaviour if a region goes down?
[07:56] Samir: automatic fallback to a secondary region with model variant or lower-cost option; Optimize can plan fallback policies that trade quality for availability.
[08:05] Jordan: switching back to the workbook — here's a sample line item: prefetch cost is computed as prefetch_rate * prefetch_cost_per_call; net savings = (hit_rate_increase * token_cost_savings) - prefetch_cost. simple algebra but useful.
[08:20] Eva: can you email the workbook after the call?
[08:22] Jordan: yes — action item.
[08:24] [small cross-talk]
[08:27] Markus: quick question on metrics — do you provide token-level breakdowns per route?
[08:31] Samir: yes, Console can break down by route/model/token buckets and show heatmaps. that helps identify high-cost prompts and where to apply caching or model distillation.
[08:42] Eva: about quality monitoring — if we quantize to 4-bit and apply prefetching, will Optimize flag regressions?
[08:48] Jordan: Optimize ties evals to prompt sets. if you see a regression above a threshold we can alert and auto-roll back to the previous model or to a fallback variant.
[08:58] Sara: great. i'm also thinking about procurement timelines — we might need SOC2 docs and an enterprise contract by mid-April. is that feasible?
[09:05] Jordan: yes; we can start with hosted free tier while you evaluate. SOC2 security pack + private deployment options usually take a few weeks for review; contracts are negotiable in parallel.
[09:16] Eva: what about costs — can you give us a ballpark monthly for our expected 450 qps baseline + 2x peaks, with moderate caching?
[09:25] Jordan: rough estimate from the sim: with moderate caching and mixed batching, think on the order of low-to-mid five figures per month; exact depends on model family and quantization. we'll provide a detailed breakdown.
[09:38] Markus: any limits on what we can instrument? we need to forward logs to our SIEM and keep logs for 365 days.
[09:44] Samir: log retention add-on available; we can stream to your S3 or SIEM and keep for 365 with the enterprise package.
[09:52] Eva: ok good. can you talk about the pilot scope — what's a minimal pilot to prove the savings?
[09:58] Jordan: minimal pilot: 2-week sandbox with your real traffic replayed against the Optimize sim (non-prod keys), run two runs: baseline (no-prefetch, default batching) and optimized (prefix cache TTL 10m, targeted prefetch, dynamic batching + route-level policy). measure p50/p95, token cost, and cache hit rates.
[10:18] Sara: sounds reasonable. can Samir run a quick bench today?
[10:22] Samir: yes I can kick off a small bench if you give a dev key.
[10:26] Eva: i'll create one after the call.
[10:29] Jordan: perfect.
[10:31] [pause]
[10:35] Jordan: now some nuanced recommendations from experience: 1) treat conversatinal flows with adaptive TTLs — shorter by default but extend on explicit user intent; 2) prefer prefetch when you have high short-term return probability signals; 3) pin critical routes to low-batch fast path; 4) run small-scale evals after quantization.
[10:55] Markus: are there any gotchas with the continuous batching runtime? we saw some threads about KV cache corruption in an older release.
[11:02] Samir: we've fixed the major issues in last two releases. the runtime has safeguards and KV eviction heuristics. we'll share release notes. if you want, we can run a tech-deep-dive with your infra team.
[11:15] Eva: yes a technical deep dive would be good. include our infra folks.
[11:19] Jordan: noted.
[11:21] Sara: ok, can we also see an example of fallback policy if the dedicated pool fills? i want to see how graceful degradation looks.
[11:28] Samir: quick summary: we can route to a lightweight model or to another region, and you can configure percent of traffic to degrade. we'll show a sample policy in the playbook.
[11:40] Jordan: wrapping up the console demo: here's where you export the simulation to spreadsheet and the button to deploy route policies to staging.
[11:50] Eva: thanks that's helpful.
[11:52] Jordan: any other open questions?
[11:55] Markus: just one on monitoring: can you correlate cache hit rate spikes to particular user cohorts?
[11:59] Samir: yes cohort-level metrics supported. you can annotate traffic and correlate.
[12:05] Eva: timeline check — we want pilot by end of March, procurement mid-April. is that doable?
[12:11] Jordan: yes pilot by end of March works if we get the traffic profile and dev key early next week.
[12:18] Eva: will do.
